common_name: Etoile Rose Clematis (Nodding Cerise-Pink Bell-Form Texas Clematis)

planting.note: Set out in spring with the crown planted a couple of inches deep and the roots shaded, allowing the slender stems to twine up a trellis, obelisk, or fence in full sun; Etoile Rose is a Texensis-type clematis with nodding, semi-double cerise-pink bell flowers.

directions: Grow this Texensis-type clematis on a narrow support such as an obelisk or wire trellis, keeping its roots cool and shaded beneath low plantings. From summer into early autumn it produces nodding, bell-shaped, semi-double flowers in vivid cerise-pink with recurved petal tips, a fuller, more textured bloom than the simple tulip-shaped flowers typical of most Texas clematis hybrids. Because it blooms on new growth, cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter to renew vigor. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many large-flowered clematis, making it a good choice for warmer gardens.

common_name: Warszawska Nike Clematis (Velvety Reddish-Purple with Silver Reverse)

planting.note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below soil level, shading the root zone while the vine climbs a trellis, arbor, or fence into full sun; Warszawska Nike, a Polish-bred Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit cultivar, bears velvety reddish-purple flowers with silvery undersides.

directions: Bred in Poland and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, Warszawska Nike bears large, velvety, deep reddish-purple flowers with silvery-mauve undersides and bright yellow stamens, opening from early summer through fall on a vigorous, free-flowering vine. Its rich, saturated color and long bloom season have made it one of the most widely planted purple large-flowered clematis cultivars worldwide. As with other clematis, keep the roots cool and shaded (mulch or low companion planting works well) while the vine itself grows into full sun, and prune according to its bloom group for the best flowering.

common_name: Emerald Zoysia Grass (Fine-Textured Golf-Course-Quality Hybrid Zoysia)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently warm; Emerald is a fine-textured hybrid between Zoysia japonica and Zoysia tenuifolia, prized for a dense, plush, golf-course-quality lawn but slow to establish.

directions: Install plugs or sod in spring through midsummer and irrigate frequently until roots knit in, then mow low, around 1 to 1.5 inches, to show off the fine texture. Emerald, a hybrid between Zoysia japonica and the fine-bladed Zoysia tenuifolia, produces an exceptionally dense, soft, dark green, needle-fine turf considered among the highest-quality ornamental zoysia lawns available, historically favored for golf courses and showcase residential lawns. It handles moderate shade better than bermudagrass and forms a dense, wear-tolerant, weed-suppressing sod once established, though its establishment from plugs is notably slower than coarser zoysia cultivars. Avoid excess nitrogen and mowing too low, both of which stress zoysia turf, and expect the lawn to go dormant and straw-colored after the first hard frost, greening back reliably each spring.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Meyer Zoysia Grass (Classic Cold-Hardy Standard Zoysia Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently warm; Meyer is the classic, longtime-standard medium-textured zoysia cultivar, valued for cold hardiness but notably slow to fill in from plugs.

directions: Install plugs or sod in spring through midsummer and irrigate frequently until roots knit in, then mow at 1 to 2 inches. Meyer has been the benchmark medium-textured Zoysia japonica cultivar for decades, valued for good cold hardiness that extends its usable range further north than many zoysia selections, along with dense, wear-tolerant, weed-suppressing turf once fully established. Its main drawback, slow establishment from plugs, has led many growers to prefer newer, faster-filling cultivars like El Toro, though Meyer remains widely available and reliable. It handles moderate shade better than bermudagrass and goes dormant and straw-colored after the first hard frost, greening back reliably each spring. Avoid excess nitrogen and mowing too low, both of which stress zoysia turf.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Argentine Bahiagrass (Broad-Leaved Low-Maintenance Pasture and Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Seed or sod in late spring through summer once soil is warm; Argentine bahiagrass has broader, darker green leaves than Pensacola bahiagrass and is more commonly used for lawns rather than pasture and roadside plantings.

directions: Seed or sod in late spring through summer once soil is consistently warm, in average to poor, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun. Argentine bahiagrass bears broader, darker green leaf blades than the more common Pensacola bahiagrass, giving it a coarser but more lawn-like appearance, and is widely used for low-maintenance home lawns, roadsides, and erosion control across the Gulf South where its deep, extensive root system provides excellent drought tolerance once established. It requires little fertilizer and tolerates poor, sandy soils that stress most other turf grasses, though its tall, wiry seed heads need frequent mowing to keep a tidy appearance. Mow regularly through the growing season, and expect it to go dormant and brown after the first hard frost.
